## Page 1

**ME 300 Homework 1: Energy Conservation and Basic Principles**

Answer the following questions neatly on a separate piece of paper or on a tablet. Written answers can be typed. Show all your work and explain your reasoning – partial credit will only be given if you show and explain each of your steps. Submit your homework on Canvas.

1. (10 points) Please fill out the energy survey on Canvas. This is a survey to get a baseline of your understanding of energy concepts at the beginning of the class. Do not look up any of the answers online!!! You will get full credit for simply answering the questions, so just do your best.

2. (10 points) Again, without looking up the answers, explain how electricity is produced and gets to your appliances. Let's use your coffee pot as an example – work back from the plug of your coffee pot all the way to the original source of energy. Where does electricity come from and does it get to your coffee pot? Answer this question to the best of your ability without any resources, it will be graded on completion only.

3. (30 points) Consider these five conservation scenarios and provide the following information about how to solve for the scenario:
   - Indicate whether it's appropriate to use a finite-time or instantaneous conservation formulation.
   - Write the form of the conservation equation, cancelling any terms that are not required and explaining why these terms can be neglected.

   a. One way to conserve water is to catch it in a rain barrel to water your plants and your lawn (https://extension.psu.edu/rain-barrels-for-water-conservation). In this scenario, a rain bucket with a volume V collects rain at a rate of $\dot{m}_{rain}$ during a rain storm. Assume that the bucket doesn't overflow. Write a conservation of mass statement for the water in this scenario.

   b. You want to make coffee using a Mr. Coffee (classic), which heats the water in the well at a rate of $\dot{Q}_{heat}$, but the coffee machine loses heat at a rate of $\dot{Q}_{loss}$. Write a conservation of energy statement for the water in this scenario.

   c. Just as you're about to make more coffee, you find coffee still in the pot from the morning – bonus! You put it in a mug and put it in the microwave for 1 minute, where $Q_{in}$ heat is added to the cup. Write a conservation of energy statement for the coffee in this scenario.

   d. Natural gas is used in a wide range of applications, from power generation to home heating. In order to move natural gas around the country, there is a network of gas pipelines where gas flows from wells to local distribution networks. In order to keep the gas moving, you need to "recompress" the gas along the pipeline

## Page 2

in a gas recompression station: https://extension.psu.edu/understanding-natural-gas-compressor-stations Here, gas flows through at a rate of $\dot{m}_{gas}$ and a compressor does work on the gas to raise its pressure at a rate of $\dot{W}_{compressor}$. Write a conservation of energy statement for the gas in this scenario.

e. Penn State has a solar farm on campus that can produce up to 2 MW of power – learn more here: https://www.psu.edu/news/campus-life/story/project-provide-reliable-and-affordable-solar-generated-energy-penn-state-0/ Although our solar farm doesn't have one, many new solar installations have battery packs to store the energy. In this system, $E_{solar}$ Joules of energy would be captured by the solar panels each day and $Q_{loss}$ Joules of energy would be lost from the system through electrical inefficiencies during the same time period. During the day, the power goes out and the house uses $E_{house}$ Joules of energy. Write a conservation of energy statement for the energy in the battery during the day.

4. (30 points) Consider the five scenarios from the previous question and answer the following:
   - Indicate whether we should use a system or control volume analysis and why.
   - Draw the scenario and then draw the system or control volume
   - Label the system/control volume, boundary/control surface, and surroundings
   - Label the energy and/or mass flows in and/or out of the system/control volume

5. (10 points) Identify the proper SI unit for each property – use the book as a reference:
   a. Pressure
   b. Temperature
   c. Volume
   d. Energy
   e. Power
   f. Length
   g. Time
   h. Mass
   i. Velocity
   j. Density

6. (10 points) I like to get to know the students in my class each semester! Please tell me why you've chosen mechanical engineering as your major (or whatever your major is), and what you'd like to do in your career after college. What types of technologies are you interested in and might like to hear more about in this class? I'll read every one of these responses!

**HOMEWORK ASSIGNMENT 10**

**CYCLE ANALYSIS**

1. (10 points) Describe the difference between the Brayton cycle and the Rankine cycle, and again the difference between the Brayton cycle and the Otto cycle. Comment on both the working fluid and the structure of the systems that run the cycles.

2. (30 points) A vapor compression cycle uses R-134a as a refrigerant with a mass flow of 0.1 kg/s and runs between pressures of 0.16 MPa and 1.8 MPa. State 1 is a saturated vapor, and State 3 is a saturated liquid. The compressor has an isentropic efficiency of 90%. Use the NIST webbook to find the state points for R-134a.

   a) What is the power required to run this cycle?

   b) How much heat is extracted from the cold space?

   c) What is the coefficient of performance of the cycle? How does this compare to the Carnot COP?

   d) In an attempt to extract some work out of the cycle, you replace the throttle with a little turbine. Assuming the turbine is ideal and the pressure ratio across the turbine is the same as that of the throttle, how much work could you extract from the fluid? How does this change the heat extracted from the cold space assuming that State 1 is the same?

3. (30 points) The Taurus 60 gas turbine in the West Campus Steam Plant has a compressor pressure ratio of 12.2 and a mass flow rate of 21.5 kg/s. The combustor adds 18 MW of heat to the cycle, and the isentropic efficiency of the compressor and turbine are 0.85 and 0.9, respectively. # ME 300 Homework 2: Defining Properties and Equilibrium

Answer the following questions neatly on a separate piece of paper or on a tablet. Written answers can be typed. Show all your work and explain your reasoning – partial credit will only be given if you show and explain each of your steps. Submit your homework on Canvas.

1. (15 points) What's the difference between a thermodynamic process and a thermodynamic cycle? Define each and describe their differences. How does the state of the system change for each?

2. (30 points) To practice thinking about different types of processes, draw the following diagrams for each of the different processes. Label your axes, the two states, and the path between them, just like we did in class.
   a. Isothermal process from $1\ \text{m}^3$ to $6\ \text{m}^3$ on a T-V diagram.
   b. Isochoric process from $800\ \text{K}$ to $400\ \text{K}$ on a T-V diagram.
   c. Isobaric process from $1200\ \text{K}$ to $800\ \text{K}$ on a P-T diagram.
   d. Isothermal process from $3\ \text{MPa}$ to $1\ \text{MPa}$ on a P-T diagram.
   e. Isobaric process from $3\ \text{m}^3$ to $2\ \text{m}^3$ on a P-V diagram.
   f. Isochoric process from $200\ \text{kPa}$ to $500\ \text{kPa}$ on a P-V diagram.

3. (30 points) The concept of quasi-equilibrium is one we'll use on every single analysis throughout the semester. In this problem, we're going to extend our analysis from class on the large ship engines to car engines to determine whether a process can be considered quasi-equilibrium. Mazda is a company that has been extremely innovative in the internal combustion engine space, working to get the most power and highest efficiency of this technology. Their SkyActiv technology is a package that improves engine efficiency significantly while still making the car a lot of fun to drive – do some research online to learn how they do it. In this problem, let's consider the Mazda 3 SkyActiv (hatchbacks for the win) – [https://www.mazdausa.com/vehicles/2022-mazda3-hatchback](https://www.mazdausa.com/vehicles/2022-mazda3-hatchback).
   a. First, explain what the quasi-equilibrium assumption is and why it's important.
   b. Next, use the Mazda website to find the bore (width of the cylinder), stroke (length the piston travels over half a rotation), and maximum engine speed (referred to as "redline" on the website) of the engine. Use this information to calculate the timescale of the compression stroke at a highway driving engine speed of 2000 RPM.
   c. Use Excel or Matlab to plot the timescale of a compression stroke as a function of engine speed from 0 to the maximum engine speed.
   d. At what engine speed would the process no longer be quasi-equilibrium? Why?

4. (10 points) Explain why a diatomic molecule like oxygen – $\text{O}_2$ – has a higher specific heat than a noble gas like neon – Ne – in units of $\text{J}/\text{kmol}\cdot\text{K}$.

5. (15 points) For this question, please write a paragraph about what you learned in the Study Skills workshop session you attended. What are three things they talked about that resonated with you and why? These can be things you're doing or things you might help – explain why these strategies might help you in this course. Finally, explain the growth mindset and how you'll apply it in the context of this course and others you may be taking this summer.

1. (15 points) Throughout this class we're going to analyze the power and steam production on campus. The East Campus and West Campus Steam Plants are what are called "cogeneration plants" or "combined heat and power plants." Learn more here:
   * Campus power: https://www.opp.psu.edu/unit/steam-services
   * Combined heat and power: https://www.epa.gov/chp/what-chp

   The engine used to make the power is a gas turbine engine – learn about how a gas turbine engine works here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jqWH77oAWl. The engine in this video is very similar to the one we have on campus. In this problem, we'll be analyzing the air going through the compressor.

**ME 300 Homework 5: Heat, Work, and the First Law**

Answer the following questions neatly on a separate piece of paper or on a tablet. Written answers can be typed. Show all your work, list all your assumptions, and explain your reasoning – partial credit will only be given if you show and explain each of your steps. Submit your homework on Canvas.

1. (10 points) What does the incompressible assumption mean? Explain it in your own words.

2. (20 points) The goal of this problem is to analyze James Prescott Joule's ground-breaking experiment where he really showed the first law and wrote about it in his seminal paper, "On the Mechanical Equivalent of Heat." This problem will provide some historical context for how the first law was experimentally confirmed, and will show you calculations based on a real-life experiment that demonstrates the transfer of energy in a quantifiable way.

   a. First, do some background research on the experiment itself and sketch it on your homework. Here are some useful resources (Definitely read/watch the first three links but you are not required to read Joule's entire paper. It's absolutely fascinating, though, so if you're interested I highly encourage you to give it a read!)
      i. Some historical context: http://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200912/physicshistory.cfm
      ii. An overview of the experiment: http://twt.mpei.ac.ru/TTHB/2/KiSyShe/eng/Chapter2/2-1-Heat_Joule's-experiment-Equivalence-of-heat-and-work.html
      iii. A video of the experiment being recreated: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MBrTDKc9YZ0
      iv. Joule's actual paper: https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/epdf/10.1098/rstl.1850.0004

   b. In Joule's paper, he says that the weights he used were 58 lbs. total. The weights were lifted to 45 inches 20 times. Calculate the total change in potential energy of the weights through the experiment in Joules.

   c. Assume water is compressible and has a specific heat of c=4.187 kJ/kg-K. Using the approximation that ΔU=McΔT to estimate how much the temperature changed as a result of the weights falling 20 times. Assume the mass of the water is 7.84 lbs., as stated on page 70 of Joule's paper.

   d. Compare that temperature difference to the measurements shown in the video (or to Joule's own measurements in the paper). Why might differences arise? For hints, Joule discusses these in detail in his paper.

   e. Using the initial temperature of the water from the video and the approximation ΔU=McΔT, determine how far these weights would have to fall to boil the water.

3. (30 points) Air (M=5 kg) is trapped in a sealed piston system with a volume of V₁=1 m³ that is initially locked so that the piston can't move. The air is heated from T₁=300 K to T₂=500 K. At this point, the lock breaks, the heater goes haywire, and the piston rises in an isobaric process until the final volume of V₃=3 m³ is reached. Calculate the following knowing that R=287 J/kg-K and c_v=714 J/kg-K:
   a. The pressure, temperature, and volume of the gas at all three states
   b. The change in internal energy (units of Joules) of the gas for these two processes
   c. The work (units of Joules) done for these two processes – was work done "by" or "on" the fluid?
   d. The heat transfer (units of Joules) for these two processes.

# ME 300 Homework 6: Steady-Flow Energy Equation and Steady-Flow Devices

Answer the following questions neatly on a separate piece of paper or on a tablet. Written answers can be typed. Show all your work, list all your assumptions, and explain your reasoning – partial credit will only be given if you show and explain each of your steps. Submit your homework on Canvas.

**Problem 1.** (10 points) Describe flow work in your own words. Use the analogy from the video to help support your discussion.

**Problem 2.** (20 points) A variable-area nozzle is used to accelerate steady-flowing air ($c_p = 1001$ J/kg-K) to different flow velocities. The air always enters the nozzle at a velocity of 10 m/s, a temperature of 350 K, and density of 1.225 kg/m$^3$, where the nozzle has an initial area of 0.02 m$^2$.

- a. What is the mass flow of air through the nozzle?
- b. Plot the temperature of the air leaving the nozzle as a function of nozzle exit velocity from 20-200 m/s. Show your calculation steps on your homework paper and then use Excel or Matlab to do the calculations at all the points requested.

**Problem 3.** (15 points) A throttle is used to reduce the pressure of steady-flowing water in a processing plant. The water enters the throttle at a pressure of 5 MPa as a saturated vapor and leaves the throttle at a pressure of 3 MPa. --- source: me300/syllabus/ME300_Su23_Syllabus.pdf pages: 7 kind: syllabus transcribed_by: deepseek-flash (from page images) --- ## Page 1 # ME 300: Engineering Thermodynamics ## Summer 2023 Instructor: Dr. Jacqueline O'Connor Associate Professor of Mechanical Engineering E-mail: [jxo22@psu.edu](mailto:jxo22@psu.edu) Office: 111 Research East Phone: 814.863.1502 The best way to get me outside office hours is by e-mail – [jxo22@psu.edu](mailto:jxo22@psu.edu). Please do not use Canvas email – I will respond much more promptly if you use my PSU email account. Course book: Turns, S. R., & Pauley, L. L. (2020). Thermodynamics: concepts and applications. Cambridge University Press. Course modality: This is a fully online course and except for the three exams will not have required class meetings. Office Hours: TBD by vote Pre-requisites/Co-requisites: CHEM 110 and MATH 141 COURSE DESCRIPTION: This course covers thermodynamics concepts, properties of pure substances, and the first and second law analysis of systems and control volumes. The objective of this course is to prepare engineering students to effectively solve theoretical and applied thermodynamics problems. Multiple forms of assessment will be used throughout the course in order to evaluate student learning. In addition, multiple professional skills will be practiced and demonstrated throughout the course, such as engineering communication and teamwork, since these skills are important in all engineering professions. By the end of this course, students will be able to: 1. Obtain thermodynamic data necessary to solve thermodynamic problems and when necessary use appropriate approximations. These skills include the use of equations of state and/or tabulated property tables. 2. Write the First Law of Thermodynamics in both appropriate forms for both closed system and control volume problem. 3. Solve problems requiring First Law analysis that produce a simple single answer. 4. Make appropriate assumptions when applying the First Law to a "real-world" problem. 5. Write the Second Law of Thermodynamics in the appropriate forms for both closed system and control volume problem. 6. Apply the Second Law to determine the performance limitations of a given thermodynamic system. 7. Apply thermodynamic concepts to describe the performance of the individual components of an engineering system, e.g., a power plant, a jet engine, and then relate that information to the overall performance of the entire system. 8. Physically interpret and apply integrals and derivatives to solve thermodynamic problems. 9. Translate complex word problems into an orderly and logical problem-solving approach. 1 ## Page 2 Dr. O'Connor reserves the right to alter or change this syllabus at any point in the semester. If this should occur, Dr. O'Connor will post an updated syllabus on Canvas and email it to the entire class. It is each student's responsibility to check their email and Canvas frequently, as well as to pay attention in class to stay up to date on any changes. COURSE PHILOSOPHY: This is a 12-week course on engineering thermodynamics in an asynchronous delivery method. The course is loosely designed based on the theory of competency-based learning, which is centered around achieving understanding for each student. Assignments are designed in both their structure and execution to act primarily as learning tools, not assessments. In particular, homework, quizzes, and "explained examples," will be used to provide student with ample opportunity to practice and master concepts before being assessed on them in three exams throughout the semester. The course also incorporates many aspects of [Universal Design for Learning], which provide students with many avenues by which to learn and practice the material. Lectures are presented in short videos with activities built into the video, and the same material is also provided in annotated slides and the textbook. Some of these aspects of the course may feel new, but they have been designed using evidence-based practices and student learning at the core. Dr. O'Connor would like to acknowledge Dr. Andrea Gregg, Assistant Teaching Professor in Mechanical Engineering and an expert in online pedagogy, for her help with the design of this course. Additionally, the images in the videos, if not otherwise stated, are subject to Creative Commons Usage. While this is an online course, I hope to create a community to support our learning. Some assignments will be interactive, and Dr. O'Connor will be available for office hours each week. Study groups are strongly encouraged, and while most of the assessments will be personal, a collegial environment is most representative of the working situations in which modern engineers will find themselves. Use the introduction videos in the first discussion board to help meet your classmates! COMMUNICATION POLICIES: Because part of becoming a professional in engineering is learning to effectively communicate, I expect that all elements of communication between students and with me as an instructor be conducted with respect. All emails sent to me must subscribe to professional expectations for communication, including a salutation, clear emails in full sentences that are grammatically correct and have been spell-checked, communicate clearly how you would like me to assist you, and end with a respectful closing followed by your name. I request that you call me Dr. O'Connor or Professor O'Connor, and address me as such in emails and in person. If your emails with me do not subscribe to these requirements, I will kindly request that you revise your emails and re-send it to me before I will respond to your email. You are welcome to email me at any time, however, I will be most responsive to emails during business hours. Although you may receive emails from me on weekends/holidays/evenings, I reserve the right to not be "on call" outside of working hours. All emails should include ME 300 in the subject line, as well as the subject of the email in order so I can quickly scan my emails. I will respond within one full business day to emails. Please do NOT use the email through Canvas – I cannot check that as often. 2 ## Page 3 TYPES OF ASSIGNMENTS — Homework: Homework is due weekly on Fridays (except on exam weeks). The best method to approaching the homework is to do as much as you can on your own, then attend office hours, post on the discussion board, or speak with your peers. Students are responsible for the material in the homework and so working the material out on your own will maximize your learning. Exam questions will closely resemble homework questions. — Explained Examples: Three times during the semester, each student will be paired with another student and will complete an "explained example." These assignments are based on a fantastic study by Brent and Felder (original paper is available on Canvas) that showed that students developed deeper understanding of concepts by explaining worked examples to each other, rather than just watching the professor do the example. In the first part of this assignment, students will record a Zoom meeting with each other and explain the example step by step, switching presenters as indicated in the assignment. Students will turn in the recording, graded for completion. The second part of this assignment requires students to review the video of Dr. O'Connor solving and explaining the same example. Students will then write a reflection comparing their step-by-step explanation to that of Dr. O'Connor's. This will be submitted the following week. Given the dynamic nature of the engineering profession, learning how to learn is an essential skill for success. This part of the assignment emphasizes metacognitive reflection and gives students an opportunity to reflect on their own thinking processes, identifying both strengths and areas in need of improvement. — Quizzes: Quizzes will be online in Canvas and are individual efforts. These are short open-book, open-note check-ins on the material covered in the videos and the book to ensure that the student understands the basics. Students are able to take each quiz three times, and the final score will be the average of the attempts. The questions may change from one attempt to the next, but the same concepts will be quizzed in each question each time. — Exams: Exams are individual efforts and will be held three times in the semester, dates below; they will be administered synchronously on Zoom. These are open-book, open-note exams that will last 1.5 hours, with 15 minutes after the exam finishes to upload written work. Exams will include both concept questions and worked problems; practice exams will be provided with solution ahead of the exam. The final exam is not cumulative, although each concept in the course builds on previous concepts, and so in a sense, all exams are cumulative. I take academic integrity during exams very seriously, which is why the exam is proctored and all students will have to sign an academic integrity pledge at the beginning of the exam. However, I do not think that the use of AI-based proctoring is fair or conducive to a productive test-taking environment.
